books.title: Master shots_ 100 advanced camera techniques to get an expensive look on your low-budget movie.pdf

theory_units.title: Motivated Camera Movement
theory_units.summary: Every camera movement must serve a deliberate narrative or emotional purpose, rather than being deployed arbitrarily for the sake of apparent excitement.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning or executing any shot involving camera movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Elevates a scene from a mere 'journeyman' effort to something 'truly great' by imbuing movement with meaning and purpose.
theory_units.caution: Never move the camera just because it's possible or to create artificial excitement; conversely, avoid static shots out of laziness or lack of thought.

theory_units.title: Director's Lens Choice Responsibility
theory_units.summary: Directors are encouraged to gain a fundamental understanding of lens choice and its effects to accurately plan shots, choreograph actor-camera dynamics, and ensure actor performances are captured effectively.
theory_units.applies_when: During pre-production planning or on-set decision-making for any shot where visual impact, framing, or actor portrayal is critical.
theory_units.expected_effect: Improved shot planning, more cohesive visual storytelling, and ensuring actor performances are done justice through optimal framing and perspective.
theory_units.caution: Solely deferring lens choice to the Director of Photography without personal understanding can result in random or potentially meaningless shots and scenes.

theory_units.title: Long Lens Stunt (Fight Scene Punch)
theory_units.summary: To create a convincing on-screen punch without physical contact, have one actor punch beside the other's head, leveraging a long lens to artificially foreshorten distances and make the punch appear to connect.
theory_units.applies_when: Staging a violent punch in a fight scene where realism and actor safety (no actual contact) are paramount.
theory_units.expected_effect: A highly convincing and impactful illusion of a punch landing, even when there is no physical contact, enhancing the scene's visceral feel.
theory_units.caution: Using the wrong lens will break the illusion, making the shot appear unrealistic or 'ludicrous'; precise actor timing for the reaction is critical for success.

theory_units.title: Speed Punch Simulation
theory_units.summary: Create the impression of a single, extremely powerful punch ending a fight instantly by choreographing the punch to occur behind the victim's head and using dynamic camera movement.
theory_units.applies_when: When the story requires a rapid fight where one punch tells the whole story, emphasizing its perfection and force.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience perceives the punch as extraordinarily powerful and decisive, making even safe stunts look strong.

theory_units.title: Avoiding Victim Perspective
theory_units.summary: Avoid camera angles that place the audience in the victim's shoes or too close behind the victim, especially when aiming for hero support.
theory_units.applies_when: When the intent is for the audience to cheer for the hero rather than empathize with the victim, especially in a decisive hero action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains audience focus and support for the hero, preventing undesirable emotional identification with the victim's perspective.
theory_units.caution: Avoid over-shoulder shots from behind the victim or angles that make the audience feel like the victim of the attack.

theory_units.title: Matching Motion for Brawling
theory_units.summary: Enhance realism and audience immersion in a fight by having the camera's motion directly follow the actors' movements, particularly during brawling or dragging sequences.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting a traditional movie fist fight as dated and desiring the audience to feel 'really there' and engaged in the struggle, especially when actors are brawling or dragging each other.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience feels more immersed and connected to the painful and dangerous action, better understanding the ebb and flow of the fight.

theory_units.title: Disguised Single-Shot Knock Down
theory_units.summary: Create the powerful visual of a character being dramatically knocked to the ground in a single shot by combining a faked punch and a gentle sit-down with a synchronized camera drop, using the attacker to shield the victim's movement.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character being knocked to the ground is a powerful storytelling moment to show defeat, but safety or budget precludes dangerous stunts, and a single, uncut shot is desired over a 'staged' cutaway.
theory_units.expected_effect: Convincingly portrays a dramatic knock-down without cuts or danger, signaling the character is losing the fight.
theory_units.caution: Requires precise timing between actor's gentle movement and camera drop; the attacker's continued aggressive movements are key to audience misdirection.

theory_units.title: Editing Kicks for Impact
theory_units.summary: Create convincing and impactful kicks in a fight scene by shooting with the edit in mind, cutting at the precise moment of impact between an aggressor's faked kick (hitting padding off-screen) and a victim's recoiling reaction (simulating the end of a kick).
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting powerful kicks, especially during a build-up to defeat or after a fight, without complex stunt work, and aiming to emphasize one character's upper hand.
theory_units.expected_effect: Kicks appear extremely effective and painful, enhancing the perception of the aggressor's dominance and the victim's defeat, all while maintaining actor safety.
theory_units.caution: Avoid having the actor kick thin air. The victim's reaction shot will look fake by itself without sharp editing and sound.

theory_units.title: Elevated Fight for Floor Close-ups
theory_units.summary: To effectively capture close-ups of characters' faces during a fight on the floor, especially to show power imbalance or emotions, elevate the actors onto a platform or table, allowing the camera to be placed below them at an optimal distance and angle.
theory_units.applies_when: When characters end up on the floor and it's crucial to show the imbalance of power, the intimacy of the confrontation, or capture the emotional climax of the fight with clear facial expressions, particularly of the uppermost character.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for clear, powerful close-ups of character faces, effectively conveying emotions of victory or defeat and the power dynamics, without distorting lenses or being too close to the actors.
theory_units.caution: Ensure great care and ample padding around the table. Do not carry out complex choreography on the raised table; reserve for close-ups at the fight's end.

theory_units.title: Off-Screen Implied Violence
theory_units.summary: To show a violent attack and the attacker's intensity without depicting explicit gore or impacts, position the camera to frame the attacker's actions and face while the victim and actual impact are concealed off-screen or replaced by padding.
theory_units.applies_when: When the film requires a strong implication of violence and extreme anger without descending into a 'gore movie,' preserving actor safety and focusing on the attacker's character/energy.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a powerful sense of violence and attacker's character/anger through implication and direct view of their face, allowing the audience to imagine the severity without explicit visuals, making it more impactful than relying on stunts and cuts.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the victim actor safely rolls out of the way and is replaced by padding for the attacker to hit.

theory_units.title: Contrastive Framing for Moment of Defeat
theory_units.summary: To clearly signal the end of a fight and emphasize the victor's dominance and the loser's defeat, use contrasting lighting, lens choices, and framing for each character, culminating in the loser leaving the frame to refocus on the hero.
theory_units.applies_when: At the very end of a fight, when it's crucial to show a clear winner and loser, and to allow the audience to relish the victory or refocus on the hero's emotions as the fight concludes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually distinguishes the victor and victim, amplifies their emotional states, and clearly signals the end of the conflict, allowing the audience to process the hero's experience without distraction.
theory_units.caution: The choice between long/short lens for the victim depends on story requirements and desired effect.

theory_units.title: Travel with Subject: Unseen Pursuer
theory_units.summary: Maintain the camera close to a struggling character in difficult terrain, without showing the pursuer, to create terror from the unseen threat and strong audience affinity.
theory_units.applies_when: When a chase has been established and the goal is to amplify terror and audience affinity to the pursued character, especially in difficult, winding terrain with frequent changes of direction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Strong audience affinity to the character's struggle, heightened terror from the unseen threat, and a sense of exaggerated movement and vastness of the background.
theory_units.caution: Only effective after the chase has already been established and the audience knows the character is being pursued.

theory_units.title: Long Lens Pan: Diagonal Chase
theory_units.summary: Pan with a character running across the screen while the attacker runs directly towards the camera, using a long lens to enhance environmental movement and foreshorten distances.
theory_units.applies_when: When the main character has a clear goal they are heading towards, and the attacker can come at them from the side, to create a unique and original sense of fear.
theory_units.expected_effect: An enhanced perception of speed and dynamic movement through the environment; attackers appear dangerously close due to foreshortening, generating a unique sense of fear.
theory_units.caution: Won't work in all story situations. Requires attackers to be clearly visible (multiple in a busy scene, or a single attacker in a quieter environment).

theory_units.title: Passing Through Tight Spaces: Increasing Tension
theory_units.summary: Increase chase tension by having a character move through a genuinely narrow space, using specific camera positioning and a short lens to exaggerate movement and environmental constriction.
theory_units.applies_when: When you want to raise tension in a chase, implying its conclusion or the imminent capture of the character, particularly in a genuinely narrow location or set.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience feels rising tension and anticipation that the character will be caught; an exaggerated sense of character speed and environmental claustrophobia.
theory_units.caution: While short lenses can make spaces look bigger, careful composition is needed to ensure the effect of filling the screen with walls and making the space feel constricting.

theory_units.title: Open Spaces: Illusion of Catching Up
theory_units.summary: Create the illusion of an attacker gaining on a hero in open spaces, even if the physical distance doesn't change, by using two cameras moving at different speeds with specific lens choices.
theory_units.applies_when: In open chase scenes where the hero has a visible goal, and you want to convey a sense of imminent capture without the attacker actually closing the distance.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience feels intense urgency and the psychological sensation that the hero is about to be caught, even if visually the distance between characters remains constant, creating subtle but powerful fear.
theory_units.caution: This effect relies on subtle differences in camera speed and lens choices to create a 'feeling' of catching up, rather than a direct visual representation.

theory_units.title: Surprise Encounter: Jolt of Fear
theory_units.summary: Create a moment of suspense and shock by showing a hero momentarily at ease, then revealing the unseen enemy with a low camera angle and a delayed point-of-view cut.
theory_units.applies_when: During a chase scene when you want to create a momentary lull of false security, followed by a sudden jolt of fear and the re-engagement of the chase.
theory_units.expected_effect: A sudden shock for the audience, intense anticipation and fear, and the chase feels re-energized with increased stakes.
theory_units.caution: The hero must plausibly be unaware of the enemy's presence for the moment of false security to be effective.

theory_units.title: The Unseen Attacker: POV Fear
theory_units.summary: Build intense fear from an unseen attacker using sound, then transition to the attacker's low-angle, short-lens point of view, creeping towards the victim.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming to maximize audience fear of an unseen threat and create a shocking, predatory perspective after establishing sympathy for the victim.
theory_units.expected_effect: Extreme psychological fear of the unknown; the audience feels like the creeping attacker, and the victim's escape seems futile due to the attacker's apparent speed.
theory_units.caution: Requires initial shots establishing the victim's fear and vulnerability for audience sympathy; starting directly with the attacker's POV might alienate the audience.

theory_units.title: The Closing Attacker: Breaking POV Expectation
theory_units.summary: Subvert audience expectations during a POV-like chase by having the attacker suddenly enter the frame from behind and grab the victim, rather than continuing the chase.
theory_units.applies_when: During a chase scene where the camera is following closely behind a fleeing character, and you want to deliver a sudden, unexpected jolt of fear to the audience by breaking cinematic convention.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience is shocked and jumps, as their established expectation of a prolonged chase is abruptly shattered by the attacker's sudden appearance and action.
theory_units.caution: Requires quick execution (only a few seconds long) to prevent audience anticipation. Relies on the audience having an established expectation of a typical chase progression.

theory_units.title: Unfair Speed Gain: Jolt of Disorientation
theory_units.summary: Generate a jolt of fear by using editing and a long lens to make an attacker appear to have made an impossible, sudden gain in distance while briefly out of sight.
theory_units.applies_when: When a hero is hiding or pausing during a chase, and you want to create a sudden, unsettling escalation of threat by making the attacker seem unnaturally close.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience experiences a jolt of fear and disorientation, perceiving the attacker as supernaturally menacing, and the chase escalates with increased urgency.
theory_units.caution: Requires the attacker to briefly disappear from sight. The effect is often more sinister if the attacker is walking rather than running.

theory_units.title: Almost There: Trapped Urgency
theory_units.summary: Create fear and urgency by showing characters on the verge of escape who are suddenly trapped, while an attacker is revealed, especially when the stakes are high.
theory_units.applies_when: When getting caught would mean instant death or the failure of a quest, and you want to evoke a strong sense of fear and desperation.
theory_units.expected_effect: A heightened sense of urgency, dread, and the frightening sensation that the attacker is inevitably gaining the upper hand, even if not in direct pursuit.
theory_units.caution: The attacker doesn't need to be in active pursuit; merely getting up or being distant can still be extremely powerful. Ensure the obstacle is genuinely difficult.

theory_units.title: Footwork: Innocent Pursuit
theory_units.summary: Capture the energy and distance of an innocent chase by using a low camera angle focused on the characters' feet, with smooth camera movement slightly faster than the pursuing character.
theory_units.applies_when: When one character is trying to catch up with another for innocent reasons, and the pursued character is unaware. Can also be adapted for secret, more serious pursuits.
theory_units.expected_effect: Forces the audience to interpret the character's emotion purely through their movement and distance, providing a smoother, more engaging view than over-the-shoulder or wide shots.
theory_units.caution: Do not stay in this shot for too long to avoid audience frustration. This shot works best as part of a sequence, preceded by shots establishing the nature of the chase.

theory_units.title: Character Switch: Heroic Entrance
theory_units.summary: Introduce a main character by having them emerge from a crowd to become the focal point of the shot, emphasizing their importance and active nature.
theory_units.applies_when: When introducing your main character for the first time or at a key moment to underline their heroic status and active role in the narrative.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly signals to the audience that this character is the hero, more important, interesting, and proactive than those around them, making their entrance impactful.
theory_units.caution: Avoid extras with distinctive faces or over-acting, as they can distract from the main character's entrance.

theory_units.title: Background Reveal: Surprise Entrance
theory_units.summary: Introduce a character as a surprise by revealing them in the distant background through camera movement, making their arrival feel like an intrusion.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character's appearance in a scene is meant to be a surprise to the audience or other characters, or for entrances of already well-known characters to emphasize their unexpected presence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dramatic, intrusive, and surprising feeling for the character's arrival, often highlighting their stillness and quiet observation.
theory_units.caution: The effect is lost if the character's arrival is loudly announced. The camera move should not feel forced; it should smoothly open up to reveal the character.

theory_units.title: The Turn In: Revealed Intent
theory_units.summary: Introduce a character by first showing their back or hidden face, then having them turn around to reveal themselves, often accompanied by movement towards another character.
theory_units.applies_when: When introducing a character who is about to make an important announcement, undergo a significant life change, or begin addressing their problems in a new way.
theory_units.expected_effect: Arouses audience curiosity about the character's hidden face, making the eventual reveal more powerful and signaling strength, determination, and a shift in focus or intent.
theory_units.caution: Ensure a reasonable justification for the character staring off into space (e.g., a window, balcony). Less camera movement is generally better; set marks to minimize adjustments.

theory_units.title: Object Revelation: Centered Importance
theory_units.summary: Introduce an important character by placing them dead center behind an object (like doors), which then opens or moves away to reveal them.
theory_units.applies_when: When introducing a main character for the first time in the film, or at a key moment to profoundly underscore their significance.
theory_units.expected_effect: Immediately signals the character's importance and draws the audience's full attention, enhanced by the anticipation of the opening object and the framing created by doorframes.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the character opening the object stands to the side to fully reveal the new character. Avoid too long a lens if it cuts out the crucial door frames.

theory_units.title: Window Push: Symbolic Closure
theory_units.summary: Signal closure or a character leaving a part of themselves behind by dollying the camera towards closing windows as the character exits the shot and turns out the light.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character is leaving a scene, and you want to convey a strong sense of closure, the end of a phase, or that they are leaving behind a part of themselves.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a surprising and powerful feeling of closure and finality, breaking audience expectations and emphasizing the emptiness or finality of what's left behind.
theory_units.caution: The effect is diminished if the window is already closed or the light already out. Ensure adequate lighting on the outside wall so the shot reveals a dark room rather than just going black.

theory_units.title: Scene Swap
theory_units.summary: Transition smoothly between two mini-scenes in the same location by visually connecting the exit of one character with the entrance of another within a single, continuous shot, often from the perspective of the character who remains.
theory_units.applies_when: When you want to seamlessly connect two conversations or mini-scenes taking place consecutively in the same location, avoiding awkward pauses or abrupt cuts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a natural flow between scenes, making the transition feel organic and less forced, maintaining audience engagement and immersion.
theory_units.caution: Cutting abruptly from one character to the next, even in the same location, can make the two scenes feel forced together rather than flowing naturally.

theory_units.title: The Pendulum Pan
theory_units.summary: A camera movement technique for character exits, combining a pan following the actor with a subtle forward dolly into their path, creating a profound sense of finality and closure.
theory_units.applies_when: Best used for a character's final exit from a section of the film or the entire film, when a strong, subtle sense of closure is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a powerful feeling of closure, making it seem as though the character is truly leaving for good, amplified by the move's subtlety.
theory_units.caution: Having the actor further away with a longer forward camera move can sometimes look forced and overly dramatic; use this alternative cautiously or when that specific effect is intended.

theory_units.title: Direction Shift (Entrance)
theory_units.summary: A tracking shot where characters walk with the camera, then turn to walk towards the camera as the tracking slows to a halt, introducing known characters into a new scene or film section.
theory_units.applies_when: Best used to introduce known characters into a new section of the film or a new scene, particularly effective for starting dialogue scenes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Gently brings characters into focus and a new context, suitable when the audience already knows them, making their entry feel deliberate and integrated.
theory_units.caution: The timing of the tracking move can be quite difficult and requires practice. If there is no dialogue, keep the shot relatively short to maintain engagement.

theory_units.title: Direction Shift (Exit)
theory_units.summary: A tracking shot where characters walk with the camera, then continue walking past the camera as the tracking slows, creating a sense of characters moving on rather than a final departure.
theory_units.applies_when: Used when characters are moving on to another location or part of the story, implying a continuation rather political than a definitive end, suggesting the audience will follow.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense that characters are 'moving on elsewhere' and the audience will 'catch up with them soon,' avoiding hard finality and suggesting ongoing narrative.
theory_units.caution: The timing of the tracking move can be quite difficult and requires practice. If there is no dialogue, keep the shot relatively short to maintain engagement.

theory_units.title: Subtle Dolly
theory_units.summary: A barely perceptible backward dolly shot where the camera recedes slightly as an actor creeps forward, inducing an unsettling feeling in the audience akin to backing into danger.
theory_units.applies_when: When characters are creeping through a dangerous space and the director wants to create a sense of unease or backing into danger for the audience, enhancing tension beyond acting alone.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience feels uneasy, as if they are retreating into dangerous territory, heightening tension and suspense without explicit threats. The move is subtle enough to be felt subconsciously.
theory_units.caution: If multiple actors spread out too much, it can dilute the sense of danger and the need to hide, reducing the effectiveness of the technique.

theory_units.title: The Unseen (Fear through Unexpected POV)
theory_units.summary: Generate fear and tension by withholding direct sight of a threat, instead using a still close-up of an actor's fearful reaction juxtaposed with a handheld, jerky, and unexpected Point of View shot of an innocuous, empty space.
theory_units.applies_when: During chase scenes or moments of high tension when the threat is distant or unseen, and the goal is to maintain or heighten fear without revealing the antagonist directly.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a profound sense of dread and unsettles the audience by showing a character's fear of the unseen, leading them to project their own fears onto the empty or innocuous space.

theory_units.title: Anticipating Motion
theory_units.summary: Generate tension in a chase or suspense scene by momentarily stopping the action, framing the main character in a corner, and drawing the audience's gaze to a bright, empty, yet plausible entry point where something is expected to appear.
theory_units.applies_when: During a chase or suspenseful sequence to heighten tension by making the audience intensely anticipate an imminent threat or appearance, even halting action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates intense anticipation and dread, making the eventual appearance of the threat more frightening and impactful, even if expected.
theory_units.caution: The empty space must offer a plausible entry point for the expected element; a dead-end corridor will not create the desired fear or anticipation.

theory_units.title: Push on Nothing (POV Dolly Through Empty Space)
theory_units.summary: Generate fear and tension by utilizing a Point of View shot that dollies forward through an empty, potentially unpleasant space, mirroring the unsettling human experience of anticipating a threat where none is explicitly visible.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character is moving through an eerie or unpleasant environment, and the director wants to create tension through the audience's anticipation of an unseen threat.
theory_units.expected_effect: Induces a deep sense of worry and dread in the audience, making them anticipate something frightening will appear, even if nothing actually does, by echoing a primal human fear.

theory_units.title: Widening the Space
theory_units.summary: A technique for escape scenes that transitions from an initial low, obscured shot to an over-shoulder view revealing a wide, challenging environment, raising tension and revealing obstacles.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character is trying to escape from a heavily guarded area, and you need to transition from hopeful creeping to facing a significant new obstacle, keeping tension high.
theory_units.expected_effect: Raises tension by shifting the audience from an uneasy, obscured perspective to directly confronting a daunting, wide-open challenge, preventing boredom in slow escape sequences.
theory_units.caution: Poor execution of slow escape scenes can lead to audience boredom; this technique helps mitigate that by introducing new visual challenges.

theory_units.title: Two Things at Once
theory_units.summary: A technique to create a moment of shock by lulling the audience into a false sense of security through parallel editing of two seemingly independent or slowly converging sequences, maintaining a consistent rhythm of cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: When desiring to create a sudden, abrupt, and shocking moment after the audience has been led to expect a slow progression or prolonged search.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience is surprised and 'jumps out of their seats' due to the unexpected and abrupt convergence of events, amplifying the shock.
theory_units.caution: Speeding up cuts or shortening shot lengths would build anticipation for a confrontation, which counteracts the desired effect of a false sense of security.

theory_units.title: Traces and Clues
theory_units.summary: A technique to convey the urgency of a character's desperate search by immersing the audience directly, combining shots from behind the character with POV shots, edited rapidly, with the character's reaction revealed only upon discovery.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character is desperately searching for an object or person, especially without dialogue, and you need to convey the urgency and deeply engage the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Engages the audience by allowing them to experience the search firsthand rather than merely observing the actor's expressions, making the search feel urgent, immersive, and preventing it from becoming farcical.
theory_units.caution: It helps if the audience is clear about what the character is searching for to understand the context of the POV shots. Delay the actor's reaction shot until the exact moment the object or person is found.

theory_units.title: Steps to Suspense
theory_units.summary: A method to build tension in a search scene by keeping the camera largely static, rooted to the ground, and using only panning or slight tilting to follow the searching character.
theory_units.applies_when: When suspense or fear is already established, and you want to show a character searching for something unfindable, keeping the audience interested despite minimal action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates high tension by contrasting the searching character's movement with the camera's rooted stillness, forcing the audience to focus intently on the search and the environment. Prevents the scene from becoming dull.
theory_units.caution: This technique requires pre-existing suspense or fear; otherwise, the character's actions might appear mundane (e.g., looking for car keys). Avoid excessive camera movement (e.g., Steadicam) as it diminishes tension. A payoff at the end enhances the effect.

theory_units.title: Visual Dancers
theory_units.summary: A Hitchcockian suspense technique showing both the hero and an approaching danger in the same shot, with the hero unaware, achieved by using a long lens to foreshorten distance and framing the danger to emerge from behind an obstruction.
theory_units.applies_when: When the audience needs to know about an approaching danger that the character is currently unaware of, to build a strong sense of suspense.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a plausible and heightened sense of suspense and an eerie, nightmarish feeling of pursuit, where the danger seems close yet not overtly moving, making the pursuit feel extremely real.
theory_units.caution: The distance between the hero and danger must be plausible for the character's unawareness. A long lens is essential; without it, the background danger might appear too small, diminishing the effect.

theory_units.title: Focus In (Push In)
theory_units.summary: A camera move where the camera pushes in relatively fast towards a key character to emphasize their intensity during a moment of realization or change, executed so that the camera movement is subliminal to the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: At a moment of significant internal change or emotional realization for a key character, to highlight their internal intensity and draw the audience into their feelings.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience is drawn to the character's feelings and intensity without consciously noticing the camera movement, fostering a deeper, more intimate connection to their emotional state.
theory_units.caution: The main mistake is allowing the composition to change; ensure one of the actor's eyes (preferably closest to the center) remains in the exact same part of the frame throughout the move. Avoid too tight an eyeline, as it can make the move feel forced or impede the actor. A long lens necessitates precise focus pulling.

theory_units.title: Moment of Drama
theory_units.summary: A technique for depicting overwhelming drama where the character retreats from the camera, which remains largely still (or only slightly tilts down), emphasizing their inability to cope.
theory_units.applies_when: When showing a moment of intense drama where the character is truly changed or deeply distressed and cannot cope, as an alternative to the standard dolly-in.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys the character's extreme distress and vulnerability by having them recede and appear to shrink in the frame, making the audience feel the intensity of the moment from a fixed, empathetic distance.
theory_units.caution: The camera cannot be completely stationary; a slight tilt down is necessary to keep the actor's eyes on the same horizontal line. This technique requires rehearsal between the actor and camera operator to anticipate movement.

theory_units.title: Pan and Slide for Overwhelm
theory_units.summary: A rapid dolly and pan camera move combined with a semi-circular actor movement to make the background rush past, emphasizing a character's feeling of overwhelm or a dramatic shift.
theory_units.applies_when: At the beginning of a fight scene, a dramatic showdown, or any moment where a character feels overwhelmed or a significant dramatic change is about to occur.
theory_units.expected_effect: A huge sensation of change, dizzying effect, makes the actor feel suspended in a world whizzing around them; audience feels the character's overwhelm.
theory_units.caution: Only use if followed by something truly dramatic, as this move announces a major action or change.

theory_units.title: Working the Background (Scene End)
theory_units.summary: A camera move evolving from an over-shoulder shot to a mid-shot, where the camera takes the place of a departing character, leaving another character alone with a swirling background, signifying the end of a scene or interaction.
theory_units.applies_when: At the end of a scene (conversation, fight) to show it coming to an end, leaving one character alone in a 'bewildering world'.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes a character's isolation and the bewildering nature of their world, creating a dramatic visual shift.
theory_units.caution: Requires precise camera operation, especially for the arc, to avoid getting too close to the remaining actor mid-shot.

theory_units.title: Pivot on Characters for Decision
theory_units.summary: A dramatic camera move that rushes towards and past an actor as they move forwards, widening the shot to show them entering the world, making a character's internal decision explicit and actionable.
theory_units.applies_when: To signal that a major decision has been made by a character and to show them setting off on a journey or action, turning an internal thought into an external event.
theory_units.expected_effect: Makes the character's decision crystal clear, emphasizes their commitment to action, and shows them 'swallowed up' by the world they're entering.
theory_units.caution: Timing is critical; if camera movement is off, it draws attention to itself. Ensure sufficient distance to avoid losing the actor's face when moving close.

theory_units.title: Reverse All Directions for Challenge
theory_units.summary: An actor runs past the camera then turns to face a challenge, while the camera moves towards and swings around them, culminating in a close shot to emphasize their reaction and preparation.
theory_units.applies_when: To show a character facing up to a huge challenge, running from danger then turning to confront it, or taking up a strategic position. Especially effective at the end of a lengthy shot with little prior camera movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a great sense of dynamic movement followed by a dramatic standstill, jolts the audience into realizing danger, and highlights the character's reaction and preparation.

theory_units.title: Backwards Dolly for Trapped Feeling
theory_units.summary: The camera backs away from a character at a constant distance as they try to move away in despair, creating a dynamic shot that emphasizes their feeling of being trapped and pursued.
theory_units.applies_when: To show a character feeling trapped in a moment, trying to escape but unable to do so rapidly, or being pursued.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates tension, makes the audience feel 'in the way', emphasizes the character's anguish, and reinforces the feeling of being trapped or pursued.
theory_units.caution: To emphasize being trapped, stick to a single line of movement (e.g., down a corridor) rather than complex paths.

theory_units.title: Underlining Stillness for Victimization
theory_units.summary: The camera dollies in on a still character who maintains a tight gaze, while the background and foreground extras move frantically and are out of focus, emphasizing their trapped and victimized state.
theory_units.applies_when: To show a character feeling trapped, like a victim, hemmed in by circumstances, and unable to act, while the world moves around them.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes the character's feeling of being trapped and their intense gaze, despite struggling to see through the surrounding chaos. Creates a sense of victimization.
theory_units.caution: Avoid too many extras that could hide the actor or distract if they pass each other within the frame. Best executed without a cut.

theory_units.title: Simultaneous Motion for Defeat
theory_units.summary: A two-shot sequence where an object passes in front of a character as they turn away from their goal in close-up, then cuts to the opposite side showing the object receding behind them, symbolizing their defeat or inability to act.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character tries to take action but cannot, showing their moment of defeat or their separation from their goal, especially for internalized decisions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Symbolically shows the character being 'spun around' and away from their goal by an external force, emphasizing their defeat or inability to act.
theory_units.caution: Timing is critical between the actor's turn and the object's position across both shots for seamless editing. Prop must be large enough for both frames yet nimble.

theory_units.title: Mirror Door Revelation
theory_units.summary: Reveals an observing character or new information in a single shot by reflecting them in a closing mirror-door, connecting them to the scene without a cut.
theory_units.applies_when: When revealing a third character observing a scene unexpectedly, connecting the observer directly to their observation, or when desiring distinct lighting styles for different parts of the frame without cutting.
theory_units.expected_effect: Keeps the audience engaged, makes visual revelation powerful, ensures clarity of who is doing what, connects the observer to their observation, enhances effect through contrasting lighting, provides a shock revelation of the observer.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the observing actor looks directly through the door, not straight ahead, to avoid audience detecting a false eye-line and making the shot feel wrong.

theory_units.title: Separating Revelation
theory_units.summary: Reveals new information (person or object) by initially concealing it behind other characters who then move aside, combined with a forward camera movement.
theory_units.applies_when: When introducing a character's return, revealing a significant person or object, or generally disclosing new visual information within a scene where its presence tells the story.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a convincing and planned revelation, creates a sense of the frame opening up like 'curtains being pulled apart to reveal a secret', avoids comical revelations.
theory_units.caution: If the background person or object is completely obscured at the start of the shot, the revelation can appear comical. It should be partially in view or indicated, blurred and partially shielded.

theory_units.title: Detail in the Crowd
theory_units.summary: Draws audience attention to an important character within a crowd by using a careful combination of long lens, selective focus, and distinct lighting.
theory_units.applies_when: When the audience needs to spot a specific, important character in a busy crowd scene, especially if they might otherwise get lost.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience's eye is immediately drawn to the important character, making them stand out sharply and preventing them from getting lost in the crowd.
theory_units.caution: Without this level of care (light and focus), the shot will reveal nothing, and the character will get lost in the crowd.

theory_units.title: Out of the Shadows Entrance
theory_units.summary: Creates a dramatic re-introduction or entrance for a character by revealing their face as they walk out of shadow, emphasizing their outline initially.
theory_units.applies_when: When re-introducing a character, making a dramatic entrance for a significant moment, showing a shift in drama partway through a scene, or when something major is being revealed to the character.
theory_units.expected_effect: Communicates that something major is occurring, creates curiosity about the character's emotional state, makes the character feel like they are walking into a new scene.
theory_units.caution: The audience must know who the character is from their outline; if completely hidden, it creates too much curiosity about *who* is hiding there. Avoid dollying backwards, as it makes the actor feel like they are passing through, not moving into the scene.

theory_units.title: Pull-Out Revelation
theory_units.summary: Reveals what a character has just seen and their prolonged reaction in a single, continuous shot, often involving a moving camera that shifts from tracking to an over-shoulder view.
theory_units.applies_when: When wanting to show a character's prolonged reaction and a slow dawning of realization to a revelation, when maintaining clear scene geography, and directing attention to new information.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a slow dawning of realization, which can be more dramatic than instant shock; maintains clear scene geography; directs audience attention to the character's focus; emphasizes moving into unknown territory.

theory_units.title: Parallel Track Revelation
theory_units.summary: Captures a character's reaction during a revelation by tracking parallel to their movement in the opposite direction while panning to keep them stationary in the frame, making the background rush past.
theory_units.applies_when: At the moment of revelation when it's important to clearly see the character's response, or when conveying a sensation that the character is caught up in a 'whirlwind of events'.
theory_units.expected_effect: The character remains almost motionless in the frame while the background rushes past, creating a sensation of being caught in a whirlwind of events, and keeps the actor's face in full view for emotional response. Allows for jump cuts between different lenses if framing is consistent.

theory_units.title: Moving On (Abrupt Halt)
theory_units.summary: Stops characters urgently in their tracks with a fast camera rush towards them, creating a sensation of speed brought to an abrupt halt to capture their shock and fear.
theory_units.applies_when: When characters are urgently moving or escaping and something unexpected forces them to an abrupt halt, requiring a clear display of their shock and fear.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sensation of great speed brought to an abrupt halt, intensifies the drama, focuses attention on the actors' faces by obscuring the background, and makes actors feel as though they might run over the camera.
theory_units.caution: Using too short a lens can make the effect too exaggerated; a medium to long lens works best.

theory_units.title: Eveline Change: Revealing an Approaching Character
theory_units.summary: This technique builds suspense and shares a character's surprise with the audience by having the camera subtly reveal a second character approaching the first, synchronized with the first character's gradual reaction.
theory_units.applies_when: When one character is joined by another, and the director wants the audience to share the surprise of the first character's discovery.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience feels the character's surprise in real-time, heightening the emotional impact of the revelation.
theory_units.caution: The first character's reaction should be gradual; a sudden look-up makes the camera move feel like an afterthought. Improper focus pull timing can make the main character blurry or the second character seem dreamlike.

theory_units.title: Eye Slide: Breaking Expectation and Revealing Detail
theory_units.summary: This technique uses a character's point of view (POV) to reveal unexpected information by simulating their focused attention through a longer lens and a rapid whip pan between details, effectively breaking audience expectations.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character is expecting to see one thing but sees another, and the director wants to emphasize the moment of realization and share the character's surprise with the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience shares the character's moment of surprise and understanding as details are revealed dynamically, making the unexpected information clearer and more impactful.
theory_units.caution: If only a wide shot is used, the audience may take too long to process the unexpected information, requiring a linger that reduces dynamism.

theory_units.title: Building Tension: Delayed Reveal of Empty Threat Space
theory_units.summary: This technique generates suspense by having a character stare into an empty space (like a corridor), but initially hiding that space from the audience. The camera then slides to reveal the emptiness, sharing the character's unease.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character is expecting something to appear in an empty space, and the director wants to maximize tension by delaying the audience's view of that space.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience shares the character's mounting unease and fear of the unknown, creating unbearable tension because nothing is revealed, only empty space.
theory_units.caution: This technique does not work if something is actually revealed in the corridor, as it would make the audience feel cheated for being excluded from information known to the character.

theory_units.title: Misdirection for Genuine Audience Shock
theory_units.summary: This technique aims for genuine audience surprise by building tension, offering an apparent moment of relief, and then delivering a shock. It uses a character-driven, off-screen distraction to truly misdirect the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to deliver a truly unexpected jump scare or surprise to a modern, media-savvy audience, avoiding common clichés.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience experiences a genuine, visceral shock because their attention was successfully diverted by a logical, character-driven distraction, making the actual surprise unpredictable.
theory_units.caution: Avoid cliché misdirections (e.g., character's back to empty space, mundane shock followed by real shock). Random off-screen noises are less effective; the distraction should be logical and character-driven.

theory_units.title: Fearing a Character: Fixed Eye-Line Framing
theory_units.summary: This technique enhances the fear of a villain by meticulously keeping their eyes, and often the victim's, in the exact same part of the frame throughout a scene, regardless of their movement, creating an unsettling fixed gaze.
theory_units.applies_when: When portraying a character (especially a villain) who is highly threatening or driven over the edge, and the director wants to enhance their frightening presence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates an intensely unsettling and frightening effect on the audience, as the villain's unyielding gaze feels inescapable and relentless, increasing the sense of vulnerability for the victim.
theory_units.caution: Requires precise camera operation to compensate for actor movement. The 'jump cut' feeling between minor adjustments can add to the effect. Actors may need to limit head and body movement.

theory_units.title: Fearing a Place: Character Trapped, Gaze to Empty Space
theory_units.summary: This technique conveys a character's profound unease and fear of a location by positioning them against a wall (feeling trapped) while they gaze past the camera into an empty, dark space, which is then revealed from their POV.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to convey that a character is afraid of a specific place, or what might be in it, rather than a person or monster.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience shares the character's feeling of being trapped and their fear of the unseen within the empty space, creating a strong, lasting moment of unease.
theory_units.caution: Do not shoot the POV shot from behind the actor; the actor should not be seen in the shot that reveals the empty space, as it's meant to be the character's perspective.

theory_units.title: Wide Spaces: Stepping into the Unknown
theory_units.summary: This technique uses wide-open spaces to generate fear by showing characters walking into an area where light diminishes, then abruptly moving off a visible or metaphorical path, with the camera tracking, but letting them move out of frame, signifying entry into the unknown.
theory_units.applies_when: When characters are truly taking a significant step from safety/known into danger/unknown, especially in a wide, exposed environment.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience feels the dramatic shift from the known into the frightening unknown, sharing the characters' sense of vulnerability and impending danger.
theory_units.caution: The timing of the camera track is critical; it must begin *at the moment* actors move off path. The camera should start still and then move, and deliberately allow actors to move out of frame to emphasize the 'unknown' aspect.

theory_units.title: Visual Shock via Refilled Empty Space
theory_units.summary: Create fright by misdirecting the audience and then revealing an unexpected element in a previously empty space within a single, continuous shot, without cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: When creating a sudden scare or jump-scare in a continuous shot, especially when a character is being pursued or is in a vulnerable state.
theory_units.expected_effect: A strong sense of surprise and fright (jump scare) for the audience, as the unexpected element appears where previously nothing was.
theory_units.caution: The empty space must be shown first. If the surprise is anticipated or the initial framing gives it away, the effect is lost. Avoid large, empty spaces around the actor initially.

theory_units.title: Shielding Attacker via Implausibility & Distraction
theory_units.summary: Generate surprise by diverting audience attention to a high-stakes, seemingly unrelated character struggle, while making the attacker's physical arrival appear impossible or highly unlikely until the moment of their sudden reveal.
theory_units.applies_when: When you want a sudden, shocking reveal of an attacker, particularly in a confined or seemingly secure space, making their appearance seem to defy logic.
theory_units.expected_effect: A complete surprise and a 'jump-out-of-their-seat' effect from the audience, as their expectations are confounded by the attacker's implausible arrival.
theory_units.caution: The misdirection must be strong enough to genuinely distract the audience. The attacker's arrival must initially seem impossible to achieve the maximum effect.

theory_units.title: Window of Fear via Distracted Movement
theory_units.summary: To make a face appearing at a window truly shocking, distract the audience by having the character engage in two simultaneous, pressing tasks that require movement, causing the window to briefly leave and re-enter the camera frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When revealing a frightening face at a window, especially when the audience might already anticipate such a reveal from an empty, dark window.
theory_units.expected_effect: A genuine shock, as the audience's attention is diverted from the window to the character's struggle, making the appearance unexpected.
theory_units.caution: The character's conflict must be plausible and demanding enough to genuinely distract the audience and cause their physical movement.

theory_units.title: Object-Guided Seamless Transition
theory_units.summary: Use a relatively insignificant object, passed between characters, to provide a natural, continuous motivation for a camera pan across a scene, connecting different areas of action without cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to move the audience's attention seamlessly and gracefully between different parts of a scene or conversations within the same location, without using a cut.
theory_units.expected_effect: A flowing, choreographed, and aesthetically pleasing shot that subtly guides audience attention while enhancing immersion and avoiding abrupt cuts.
theory_units.caution: The transition where the actor moves past the camera should be relatively brief, as it is a transition rather than a journey and not intended to hold attention for long.

theory_units.title: Handing Off Motion for Uncut Focus Shifts
theory_units.summary: In a busy scene without cuts, transition audience focus between different characters or areas of action by using a backward dolly timed with a character's movement, creating space for the next focal point.
theory_units.applies_when: In complex or busy scenes with multiple characters or story threads, where the director wants to maintain a single continuous shot and guide audience attention smoothly between points of action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhanced sense of urgency and drama, allowing the viewer to see various story threads unfold in one frame, without drawing attention to the camera move itself.
theory_units.caution: Characters must have good, realistic motivation for their movement to ensure the camera move feels natural and not artificial.

theory_units.title: Change of Direction for Dynamic Space Reveal
theory_units.summary: Reveal a sense of surrounding space or landscape dynamically by dollying backward with characters, then having one character move faster across the path of another, prompting a pan that follows them and brings the camera to rest, showing the wider environment.
theory_units.applies_when: When you want to convey a sense of a larger space or a wider landscape to the audience, using character movement to motivate a fluid, dynamic camera move rather than a simple, unmotivated pan.
theory_units.expected_effect: A dynamic and flowing sense of motion, making the audience feel they've seen the whole landscape, without the camera move itself drawing undue attention.
theory_units.caution: The faster character needs strong, realistic motivation to run; avoid having them speed up merely for the convenience of the camera move.

theory_units.title: Using Reflections for Dual Perspective
theory_units.summary: Employ reflections to simultaneously show a character's reaction and the object/subject of their attention, offering an elegant alternative to cutting between shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When you need to convey both a character's internal reaction and the external stimulus in a single, continuous frame, particularly in gentle scenes or moments of revelation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances narrative elegance, directs audience attention efficiently, and provides a richer, more immersive visual experience by combining perspectives.
theory_units.caution: Avoid cheated eyelines as they can register as 'wrong' with viewers. Lens choice is critical: wide lenses may make reflected subjects too distant; long lenses blur reflections unless focus is pulled to the background, which can be confusing if overused.

theory_units.title: The Rest Point Camera Move
theory_units.summary: A camera movement that deliberately travels towards a close-up of a main character who is reacting to a significant object, creating a powerful sense of gravity and inevitability.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character receives a physical object (e.g., a letter) that brings them to a halt, symbolizing a moment of profound revelation or impact.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a 'magnetic moment' where the camera and scene elements are drawn towards the character's emotional core, emphasizing the importance and inevitability of the revelation.
theory_units.caution: The effect is destroyed if the actor stops immediately upon receiving the object. They must initially ignore it and move off, then return to the camera's resting point.

theory_units.title: Color Guides for Attention
theory_units.summary: Utilize striking colors on key background characters or objects to direct audience attention and ensure immediate recognition, especially when the background is blurred or distant.
theory_units.applies_when: When a distant or blurred background character's identity is significant to the foreground character and requires instant audience recognition without 'slow dawning'.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides immediate visual clarity and identification of a crucial background element, effectively guiding the audience's eye and priming them for a foreground reaction.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the chosen color suits the character's personality; avoid arbitrary color choices. Overuse of strong contrast can distract if not carefully integrated.

theory_units.title: Reverse Angles for Dynamic Dialogue
theory_units.summary: Capture the natural movement and emotion of an argument or dramatic discussion by keeping the camera static in a wide master shot while blocking actors to face the camera when speaking.
theory_units.applies_when: In scenes where characters are arguing or engaged in dramatic discussion and their natural movement (circling, pacing) needs to be captured without complex camera moves.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains audience awareness of character positions while allowing for dynamic actor movement, preserving the energy and emotion of the scene without disorienting cuts.
theory_units.caution: One actor will always be facing away from the camera; they must use strong body language and acting to maintain presence. If needed, supplementary coverage of hands/feet can be used to facilitate cuts without close-ups.

theory_units.title: Front Seat Car Shooting
theory_units.summary: A low-budget car scene technique where the camera is placed in the front seat, pointing towards the back, often with a long lens to emphasize the actor's face.
theory_units.applies_when: When shooting a conversation or interaction with actors in the back seat of a car, prioritizing their performance over elaborate car rigs.
theory_units.expected_effect: Focuses attention on the actor's performance by making their face dominate the frame, while still conveying the setting of a moving car through subtle background motion.
theory_units.caution: Be mindful of actor eyelines; they may not be able to look across empty space as conventionally. Consider filling empty space in the frame (e.g., with a hand). Stabilize the camera, and drive at an abnormally slow speed.

theory_units.title: Back Seat Car Shooting
theory_units.summary: A complementary car scene technique where the camera is positioned in the back seat, capturing the driver or front seat passenger, often creating a sense of isolation for the backseat occupant.
theory_units.applies_when: When the main character is in the back seat and the focus is on their interaction with the front seat occupants, or to convey the experience of a passenger in a taxi.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes the front seat occupant's presence while subtly highlighting the backseat character's perspective, potentially creating a feeling of isolation or unsettled communication.
theory_units.caution: Drivers must still watch the road, so their interactions are limited to glances or mirror use. A longer lens is needed for mirror shots to clearly see eyes, requiring careful focus checking.

theory_units.title: Back Seat Car Dialogue Framing
theory_units.summary: A specific back seat camera setup for two-shot car dialogue, positioning the camera on the opposite side of each actor to capture their expressions as they look across at each other.
theory_units.applies_when: For capturing engaging dialogue between two actors in the front seats of a car, shot from the back without complex rigs, where eye contact is crucial.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures clear visibility of actors' expressions and their eye contact during dialogue, making the conversation feel more intense and focused.
theory_units.caution: The driver will naturally get less coverage due to needing to watch the road. Opening windows for energy can disturb sound, requiring careful audio planning or ADR.

theory_units.title: Outside Camera for Parked Car Dialogue
theory_units.summary: Positioning the camera outside a parked car with a long lens helps to isolate actors and their dialogue from surroundings, making them the primary focus.
theory_units.applies_when: When shooting scenes in a parked car and the primary focus should be on the actors and their conversation, rather than the environment.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased audience focus on the actors and their dialogue; minimizes distraction from surroundings.

theory_units.title: Actor Lean for Important Conversation
theory_units.summary: Having actors lean forward in a parked car scene can make their conversation seem important.
theory_units.applies_when: When the conversation within the parked car is truly engaging and significant to the characters.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience perceives the conversation as significant and engaging.
theory_units.caution: Only use this technique when the conversation is truly engaging; otherwise, it can feel unnatural or forced.

theory_units.title: Avoid Shooting Through Car Glass
theory_units.summary: To prevent reflections and distortions, avoid shooting through car glass by opening doors or winding down windows.
theory_units.applies_when: Whenever shooting through car windows, especially with external camera setups.
theory_units.expected_effect: Cleaner, undistorted image without unwanted reflections or glare.

theory_units.title: Minimize Actor Movement in Car
theory_units.summary: Instruct actors to minimize movement within the car to avoid foreground intrusions that detract from audience immersion.
theory_units.applies_when: When the goal is for the audience to feel intimately 'in the car' with the actors.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains audience immersion and focus on the actors without distracting foreground elements.
theory_units.caution: Excessive movement can lead to foreground intrusions (car doors, chassis) which break immersion.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Character Exit from Car
theory_units.summary: Transform the mundane act of a character leaving a car into an engaging moment by closely identifying with the actor through camera movement and framing transitions.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character's exit from a car needs to be more than just 'passing time' and should actively engage the audience, drawing them into the character's perspective.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased audience interest and identification with the character; prevents boredom during transitional moments.
theory_units.caution: Without this technique, getting into or out of a car can be boring and lose audience interest.

theory_units.title: Motivated Eyeline Near Camera During Exit
theory_units.summary: Have the actor's eyeline almost directly into the camera, framed so their point of interest appears to be behind the camera, providing natural motivation for a close connection.
theory_units.applies_when: When a close connection and identification with the character is desired, particularly during transitional movements like exiting a car.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increases audience connection and identification with the character by making the eyeline feel direct and naturally motivated.

theory_units.title: Car Walk for Character Barrier
theory_units.summary: The 'car walk' convention (one person in a moving car, another walking alongside) establishes a mild barrier between characters, which can convey sinister or sincere intentions.
theory_units.applies_when: When portraying a dynamic where one character is attempting to influence or 'coerce' another, or when highlighting a subtle separation between them.
theory_units.expected_effect: Communicates a nuanced psychological barrier or power dynamic between characters; adds emotional depth to the interaction.
theory_units.caution: The effect (sinister or sincere) depends entirely on context.

theory_units.title: Car Walk Framing Convention
theory_units.summary: Frame the exterior character hard right and the interior character to the left for a clear visual separation in a 'car walk' scene.
theory_units.applies_when: When setting up a 'car walk' shot to clearly delineate the positions of the two interacting characters.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clear visual separation and balance between the two characters in the frame.

theory_units.title: Camera Height for Character Identification in Car Walk
theory_units.summary: Camera height in a 'car walk' scene is crucial for determining which character the audience identifies with more strongly.
theory_units.applies_when: When establishing a clear point of view or identifying character in a 'car walk' sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Directs audience empathy or identification towards a specific character; clarifies power dynamics.
theory_units.caution: Using different camera heights for each direction can neutralize the scene's emotional impact or identification.

theory_units.title: Car Speed for Car Walk
theory_units.summary: Ensure the car barely moves at walking pace during a 'car walk' to allow for careful camera control and composition.
theory_units.applies_when: Always, when staging a 'car walk' scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for stable tracking and composition, ensuring the shot is visually coherent and safe.
theory_units.caution: Great care must be taken when shooting these scenes.

theory_units.title: Car Walk Driver Shot Setup
theory_units.summary: To shoot the driver in a 'car walk', set up a dolly and track slightly ahead of the car, framing the driver to the left.
theory_units.applies_when: When capturing the perspective or interaction with the driver in a 'car walk' scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a dynamic, stable shot of the driver, maintaining the desired composition relative to the car's movement.

theory_units.title: Car Walk Walker Shot Setup
theory_units.summary: To shoot the walking character in a 'car walk', place the camera in the front seat close to the windshield, framing the walker to the right.
theory_units.applies_when: When capturing the perspective or interaction with the walking character in a 'car walk' scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a stable shot of the walker from the car's interior perspective, maintaining the desired composition.

theory_units.title: Long Lens for Car Walk Separation
theory_units.summary: Use a long lens in 'car walk' scenes to separate characters from their background surroundings while retaining some car bodywork for context.
theory_units.applies_when: When emphasizing the characters and their interaction over the environment in a 'car walk' scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Shallow depth of field, drawing audience attention to the characters and the implied barrier between them, rather than distracting surroundings.
theory_units.caution: Do not cut out the bodywork of the car completely, or the shot can feel disorienting.

theory_units.title: Single Character Focus in Stake-out Car Scene
theory_units.summary: In stake-out or waiting car scenes, set up camera angles that focus on only one actor at a time, avoiding actors looking at each other or rack focus.
theory_units.applies_when: Specifically for 'watching and waiting' scenes in a car, where the tension or individual thought process of each character is paramount, not their conversation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Directs audience attention to the specific character in focus, emphasizing their individual state of anticipation or observation. Avoids confusing multiple points of interest.
theory_units.caution: If the scene is about conversation, use other setups. This approach is specifically for 'watching and waiting'.

theory_units.title: Long Lens for Farthest Actor Focus in Car
theory_units.summary: When focusing on the farthest actor in a two-person car shot, use a very long lens from a distance to make their head appear roughly the same size as the closer actor, ensuring clear focus on the intended subject.
theory_units.applies_when: When the farthest of two actors in a car is the designated focus of attention, and the closer actor should be subtly present but out of focus.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly directs audience attention to the farthest actor, while subtly indicating the presence of another character, creating a sense of selective focus and psychological distance.
theory_units.caution: Too short a lens will make the farthest actor's head appear relatively small, reducing their importance. May need to cheat by having the farther actor sit slightly forward.

theory_units.title: Front Camera for Closest Actor Focus in Car
theory_units.summary: To focus on the actor in the left-hand seat (closest to the front) in a waiting car scene, place the camera directly in front of the car and use a long lens for a close-up.
theory_units.applies_when: When the closest actor in a waiting car scene becomes the primary focus of attention.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes the closest actor's face and internal state through a focused close-up.

theory_units.title: Conversation Dolly for Intimate Power
theory_units.summary: Position characters next to each other and use a simultaneous push-in dolly from both angles to draw the audience into the intimate power of their conversation, as an alternative to cutting between facing characters.
theory_units.applies_when: When seeking an alternative to standard dialogue coverage, especially for brief, intense conversations where the aim is to create a strong sense of intimacy and power dynamics between characters.
theory_units.expected_effect: Heightened audience engagement, a feeling of being drawn into the conversation, and emphasized intimate power dynamics. Avoids tedious cutting.
theory_units.caution: A fast push-in creates too much effect; works best for relatively brief conversations. Dolly moves must happen at exactly the same speed if using multiple cameras or repeating takes.

theory_units.title: Dominant Character in Conversation Dolly
theory_units.summary: Within a 'conversation dolly' setup, one character should be visually dominant, often by looking directly at the other who avoids their gaze, to highlight power dynamics.
theory_units.applies_when: When emphasizing an imbalance of power or focus between two characters in a conversation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly communicates which character holds more power or is driving the interaction, making the power dynamic visually evident.

theory_units.title: Ending Conversation Dolly Smoothly
theory_units.summary: Ideally, let the camera come to rest a couple of beats before the scene ends, allowing for a moment to stick with one shot before cutting out.
theory_units.applies_when: When concluding a scene filmed with the 'conversation dolly' technique.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a smooth, satisfying conclusion to the scene, avoiding a rushed or forced feeling.
theory_units.caution: Cutting between moving shots after the move is over can seem forced. Cutting out while cameras are still moving feels like leaving before the conversation is over.

theory_units.title: Offset Background Dolly for Dialogue Conflict Focus
theory_units.summary: To make a dialogue scene interesting, especially when one character refuses to look at the other, use a camera move to draw focus onto this conflict, progressively isolating the key character.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting a dialogue scene where one character is resistant, stubborn, or deliberately avoiding interaction, and you want to visually emphasize this conflict and the character's internal state.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws the audience's attention to the stubborn character, isolating them and intensifying the feeling of resistance as the background 'fades away'.
theory_units.caution: The effect is strongest if the resistant character remains still.

theory_units.title: Stillness for Resistant Character in Offset Dolly
theory_units.summary: In an 'offset background' shot, if the resistant character remains still, it creates a stronger feeling of resistance as the camera tracks past them.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting a character's resistance or stubbornness in a dialogue scene with camera movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Amplifies the character's sense of internal strength and resistance to external influence; creates a powerful visual metaphor for their steadfastness.
theory_units.caution: While tempting to have the character move, the effect is strongest if they remain still.

theory_units.title: Share Screen for Naturalistic Dialogue
theory_units.summary: Show both characters simultaneously in a dialogue scene to achieve a more naturalistic and actor-led feel, as people rarely stand directly facing each other in real conversations.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming for a more realistic and less editorially driven portrayal of a conversation, allowing actor performances to dictate rhythm.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhanced sense of realism; allows audience to observe simultaneous reactions; shifts scene rhythm to actors.
theory_units.caution: The classic soap opera shot (one character facing camera, other talking to back) is a cliché and generally ineffective in films without a specific 'twist'.

theory_units.title: Orienting Actors for Share Screen Visibility
theory_units.summary: To effectively 'share the screen', carefully orient actors so both faces can be seen, ideally when seated, on different levels, or with one actor moving around the other, complemented by glances.
theory_units.applies_when: When attempting a 'share screen' dialogue shot to avoid cliché and ensure both performances are visible.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows simultaneous visibility of both actors' reactions and expressions, enhancing naturalism and performance delivery.
theory_units.caution: Without careful orientation, you can end up with the 'soap opera shot' cliché or both actors in profile, concealing performance and lessening drama.

theory_units.title: Dominant Eyeline in Share Screen
theory_units.summary: In a shared screen shot, position the camera so one actor has a reasonably direct eyeline towards it, making them the dominant point of interest and guiding audience attention.
theory_units.applies_when: When both actors are on screen simultaneously, and a clear point of audience attention or a subtle power dynamic needs to be established.
theory_units.expected_effect: Directs audience focus to the designated dominant character; helps prevent the shot from becoming bland or unfocused by having two equally important subjects.
theory_units.caution: Without care, both actors shown in profile lessens drama. The shot is potentially less dramatic because no actor is completely dominant.

theory_units.title: Camera Movement for Share Screen
theory_units.summary: Share screen shots can work with zero camera movement, but an ambitious director might move the camera and actors, even switching dominant eyeline halfway through.
theory_units.applies_when: When deciding on the dynamic level of a shared screen dialogue scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds dynamism and complexity to the shot if movement is employed; maintains simplicity and focus if static.

theory_units.title: Side-by-Side Dialogue: Apparent Disinterest
theory_units.summary: Staging characters side-by-side can make them appear disinterested in each other, especially if they are not looking at a shared off-screen focal point.
theory_units.applies_when: When characters are positioned side-by-side in a dialogue scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience perceives characters as disengaged or uninterested in the conversation.
theory_units.caution: Avoid this setup if the intention is to show characters engaged with each other's conversation without direct eye contact.

theory_units.title: Side-by-Side Dialogue: Off-Screen Shared Focus
theory_units.summary: To convey engagement between side-by-side characters without direct eye contact, have both characters look at a compelling shared off-screen object or event.
theory_units.applies_when: When characters are side-by-side and need to appear engaged with each other's conversation or a shared context, but without looking directly at each other.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience understands a shared focus and connection between characters, allowing for individual reactions to be observed.

theory_units.title: Side-by-Side Dialogue: Suppressed Glances for Impact
theory_units.summary: When characters are looking at a shared off-screen subject, minimizing glances between them enhances the power of their individual reactions and focuses attention on the dialogue.
theory_units.applies_when: When characters are arranged side-by-side, looking at a shared off-screen subject, and the director wants to emphasize dialogue and individual emotional responses.
theory_units.expected_effect: Heightened focus on the dialogue and characters' internal reactions; strengthens the connection between characters through their shared experience rather than direct interaction.

theory_units.title: Reverse Angle: Including Characters with Gaze Subject
theory_units.summary: When cutting to a reverse angle to reveal what side-by-side characters are looking at off-screen, include the characters in the shot with the subject of their gaze.
theory_units.applies_when: When characters are looking at a compelling off-screen subject and the director needs to show what they are seeing.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience remains oriented and maintains a strong connection with the characters and their shared experience of observing the subject.
theory_units.caution: Simply cutting to the subject without including the characters has the potential to disorient the audience.

theory_units.title: Reverse Angle: Height Differential for Shared Gaze
theory_units.summary: When cutting to a reverse angle to show what characters are looking at from a side-by-side setup, adjust the reverse camera's height to align with their gaze (e.g., high camera if they look down).
